1107.title: Who Wrote Lalita's Thousand Names
1107.hook: the hymn's own story: goddesses of speech compose her names, and she hands them to everyone
1107.carry: her names were given so anyone could call her
1107.howItsDone: Some devotees learn the Lalita Sahasranama from a teacher and recite it daily or on Fridays; in a temple or home archana, a name is offered with each flower or pinch of kumkum, in the form 'om … namah.'

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama held two ways of speaking side by side: won over by devotion, and without form. A new week.
screen: `NEAR, AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: The court is full. Gods, goddesses, sages and attendants are packed in before the throne of the goddess Lalita. Then the goddesses of speech step forward and begin to recite, name after name. That's the scene the Brahmanda Purana gives for where the Lalita Sahasranama came from. The whole hymn is set inside a conversation: Hayagriva, a horse-headed form of Vishnu, teaching the sage Agastya. And when Agastya hears the names, he's also told how they began, and what the goddess did when she heard them.
screen: `A FULL COURT.` → `THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.` → `WHO WROTE THE NAMES?`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in paraphrase, as the text tells it. Lalita calls the goddesses of speech, the Vagdevis, Vashini and her companions, and asks them to compose a hymn of her secret names, so that her devotees might have a way to please her. They compose it. Then one day, with the whole court gathered, the goddess signals to them, and the Vagdevis stand and recite the names they've made. The court is amazed. And the goddess, pleased, tells everyone assembled to recite it: this hymn, made at her command, is the way to her favor. Notice who starts it. Not a poet trying to climb up to heaven. The goddess herself asks for her names to be made, so her people would have a way to reach her. That's a real thread in Hindu devotion: a divine name isn't a label people stick on God. Many teachers call it a door, and here God is the one who opens it. It's why so many deities have a sahasranama, a thousand names, and why a family may offer one flower or one pinch of kumkum with each name. Tradition keeps reverence around this hymn too; some teachers say it should be received from a teacher, not picked up casually. Both live side by side. But the scene ends with the doors open. So when a grandmother sits down on a Friday and works through the names, she isn't trying to catch the goddess's attention. In the hymn's own story, the goddess handed her the way in.

segments.voice: Choose one name from the hymn that you've met this week, the one who gives grace, the one fond of devotion, the one without form, or simply the name Lalita, and say it once, quietly. Let the silence after it be as long as the name, then say it again, unhurried. If you pray, you can offer the name back to the goddess each time; if you don't, notice what a single word does when it's given room.
The Lalita Sahasranama: Lalita's thousand names. In the text's own story, composed by the goddesses of speech at her command, and given to everyone in her court.

1108.title: The Last Name Is Mother
1108.hook: the hymn's last names: Shiva and Shakti as one form, and then simply the mother, Lalitambika
1108.carry: shiva and shakti are one, and she is mother
1108.howItsDone: In recitation of the Lalita Sahasranama the closing names, Sri Shiva, Shivashaktyaikyarupini and Lalitambika, end the hymn, and in a name-by-name archana the last offering is made with the name Lalitambika.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama's own story: the goddess had her names made, and gave them to everyone. Today, the last of the names.
screen: `A DOOR SHE OPENED.`

segments.voice: Some strings of prayer beads have a larger bead where the two ends meet. Move bead by bead and the fingers come back to it: the end of the round is where it started. The Lalita Sahasranama has a shape a little like that. It opens by calling the goddess Sri Mata, the auspicious mother. And after everything in between, the hands, the war, the five acts, the climb through the body, the names of without, it closes on the mother again.
screen: `A BEAD WHERE THE ENDS MEET.` → `IT OPENS WITH THE MOTHER.` → `IT CLOSES ON HER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The final names, in paraphrase. Sri Shiva: the auspicious one, given the very name of Shiva. Then: the one whose form is the oneness of Shiva and Shakti. And last: Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Take the middle one first. Shiva and Shakti can sound like two gods, a husband and a wife. This name says something bigger, and it's a core teaching of the goddess's devotees: Shiva and Shakti are one reality. Shiva is its stillness, pure awareness; Shakti is its power, everything that moves. You can't have one without the other, and this name says that single form is hers. The poet Kalidasa, opening one of his poems, pictures the divine couple joined like a word and its meaning. Nobody can hold the meaning in one hand and the word in the other. It's the same idea people see in Ardhanarishvara, the image that's half Shiva, half Parvati, in one body. Then the very last name. Tradition hears play in the name Lalita, and amba is mother. After a noose and a goad, a war, Kama brought back from ash, a power rising through the spine, and names that say no form can hold her, the last word isn't a throne or a weapon. It's mother. That's the second teaching, and Hindus live it every day: the highest reality can be called Ma. Some devotees hear a homecoming in that ending; others hear the oneness in the name before it: the mother is the whole of reality, playing.
screen: `SRI SHIVA.` · `ONE FORM OF SHIVA AND SHAKTI.` · `JOINED LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` · `LALITAMBIKA: LALITA THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `ONE REALITY. CALL HER MA.`

segments.voice: Notice the turn at the top and the bottom of each breath: each one ends where the next begins, like beads on a string. Near the end, bring to mind someone who has looked after you, and let the breath come round to them. If you pray, you can say the name Lalitambika, or the name you use for the one who holds you, once, quietly; if you don't, let the breath be the bead.

1109.title: Where Her Story Is Told
1109.hook: the goddess makes her last promises, and night one of Navaratri gives her a seat
1109.carry: she stays where her story is told
1109.howItsDone: In many homes the first day of Navaratri begins with ghatasthapana: a water pot (kalash) with mango leaves and a coconut is installed, and the goddess is invited to dwell in it for the nine nights; in parts of North India barley is sown beside it to sprout. Elsewhere the first night opens with a lamp, dance, a display of dolls, or recitation of the Devi Mahatmya.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama closed on Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Tonight, the goddess's nine nights begin.
screen: `THE LAST WORD IS MOTHER.` → `THE NINE NIGHTS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: The last battle of the Devi Mahatmya is over. Shumbha, the demon king who took the gods' heaven, is dead, the world grows calm, and the gods sing to the goddess one more time. Then she answers them. With promises about the future: about anyone, anywhere, who will someday tell this story. Tonight, night one of Navaratri, is where those promises come home.
screen: `THE LAST BATTLE IS OVER.` → `THE GODDESS ANSWERS.` → `PROMISES ABOUT THE FUTURE.`

segments.voice: You met Navaratri on day eighty; tonight, how it opens. In the twelfth chapter the goddess makes her promises, in paraphrase. Whoever praises me with these hymns, I will take away their troubles. Where this story is recited in my shrine, I will never leave; my presence stays there. Whatever worship is offered me, by someone who knows the rules or someone who doesn't, I accept with love. And at the great worship held every autumn, whoever hears my story with devotion will be freed from troubles. Then she vanishes. Two of those promises explain how Navaratri begins. The first: her presence stays where her story is told. So on night one, in many homes, she's given a seat. A pot of water, the kalash, is set out with mango leaves and a coconut at its mouth, and with prayer the goddess is invited to dwell in it for the nine nights. In some homes in North India, barley is sown in soil beside it, and by the end the dish is green. Some families read her story across the nights. Either way, for nine nights the house becomes her shrine. The second promise is the one to hold onto if you've ever worried you're doing it wrong. Known or not known, she says, I accept it with love. Plenty of families today don't remember every step their grandparents knew. Many teachers read this verse as her answer: she looks at the devotion, not the checklist. Night one is simple. Give her a seat, and she stays.
screen: `THE GODDESS'S PROMISES.` · `WHERE MY STORY IS TOLD, I STAY.` · `NIGHT ONE: A POT, A COCONUT, A SEAT.` · `KNOWN OR NOT KNOWN, I ACCEPT IT.` · then, large: `GIVE HER A SEAT. SHE STAYS.`

segments.voice: If you keep a shrine, or even a shelf, light a lamp or a candle tonight and invite the goddess in your own words, the way families do on night one: come, Ma, stay with us these nine nights. Don't worry about saying it right; she said she'd take it with love either way. Then sit for a few breaths with the flame, as if a guest has just arrived. If you don't pray, sit with the light anyway, and notice what it's like to make room in a home for something you can't see.

1110.title: Durga, the Boat Across
1110.hook: night two: the buffalo demon has fallen, and the gods praise the warrior goddess as a boat
1110.carry: durga is the boat across samsara's ocean
1110.howItsDone: During the first nights of Navaratri, some families keep a fast, light a lamp before an image of Durga, visit her temple, or recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya, including the gods' hymn of praise in chapter four.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night one: the goddess promised to stay where her story is told, and Navaratri gave her a seat. Tonight, night two.
screen: `NIGHT ONE: A SEAT FOR HER.`

segments.voice: The battlefield has gone quiet. Mahisha, the buffalo demon who drove the gods out of heaven, lies dead, and the goddess who killed him is still standing there, weapons in all her hands. The gods, led by Indra, step forward to sing to her. You'd expect them to praise her as a sword, or a fortress. Partway through, they call her something else. They call her a boat.
screen: `THE BUFFALO DEMON HAS FALLEN.` → `THE GODS SING.` → `THEY CALL HER A BOAT.`

segments.voice: It's in the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, and the line plays on her name. In paraphrase: you are Durga, the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean of worldly life. Her name, Durga, sits right beside durga, hard to cross, the word the gods use for that ocean. The one named for what's hard to get through is the boat that gets people through it. And that ocean has a name in Hindu teaching: samsara, the round of birth, death and birth again, with all its worry and wanting. Many Hindu prayers call it bhava-sagara, the ocean of becoming, and ask God to carry them across. The gods have just watched her win a war, and they don't only praise her as a weapon. They praise her as the way across. Some readers hear her name point two ways: toward anyone who threatens her people, she's hard to get past, like a wall; toward anyone in trouble, she's the boat. That's why so many Hindus turn to Durga when life is hardest. Her fierceness faces outward, at what threatens; to the one who comes to her, she's refuge. In these first nights some devotees dwell on her battles, reading the demons as anger, pride and confusion, and keep a fast or recite the chapters; others put the weight on the boat, and simply come to her temple, or her lamp, with what they can't carry. The second night asks: what are you trying to cross alone?
screen: `THE GODS SING AFTER THE VICTORY.` · `DURGA, BESIDE HARD TO CROSS.` · `SAMSARA: THE OCEAN OF BECOMING.` · `FIERCE OUTWARD, REFUGE INWARD.` · then, large: `THE BOAT ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels hard to cross this week and look at it plainly. Then ask: am I trying to swim this alone? If you pray, bring it to Durga, or to God, in your own words, the way the gods did: you are the boat. If you don't, think of one person or one practice that could carry you part of the way, and let that be enough for tonight.

1111.title: Whenever We Remember You
1111.hook: night three: the gods are offered any boon, and ask only that she come whenever they remember her
1111.carry: remember the goddess, and she comes again
1111.howItsDone: Some devotees recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya during Navaratri, or in times of trouble, holding to the gods' boon in chapter four that the goddess will come when she is remembered.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night two: the gods praised Durga as the boat across samsara's ocean. Tonight, night three.
screen: `THE BOAT ACROSS.`

segments.voice: Choose a boon. The path heard the goddess say it to the gods earlier this year, reading the Devi Mahatmya whole. The buffalo demon is dead, and the gods could ask for anything: riches, safety forever, a share of her power. Tonight is night three, the last of the nights that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga. And that old request, from the end of the fourth chapter, turns out to be the root of something Hindus do every day.
screen: `CHOOSE A BOON.` → `HEARD BEFORE.` → `THE ROOT OF A DAILY PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in paraphrase. Everything has already been done for us, they say, because our enemy is dead. But if you'll give us a boon, then whenever we remember you again, destroy our worst troubles. And be gracious to anyone who praises you with these hymns. The goddess agrees, and vanishes. Look at what they didn't ask for: not a fortress that would last forever, not a guarantee that nothing bad would happen again. As if they know it will. Heaven has been lost once; it can be lost twice. So they ask for a promise of return: remember me, and I'll come. That's a big teaching, and it has a name: smarana, remembering God. In Hindu devotion, calling the divine to mind, by name, by hymn, by a picture on the wall, isn't just thinking about her. It's how she's called. That's why some families recite the Devi Mahatmya, the Chandi path, every Navaratri, and again in hard times: the reciting is the remembering the gods asked for. It's why a grandmother says the goddess's name under her breath in a hospital corridor. Some devotees take the promise literally: in trouble, recite, and she comes. Others read it inwardly: the remembering is itself the help, the moment a person turns toward something larger than the mess in front of them. And the circle is wide. The gods don't ask only for themselves, but for anyone who sings these hymns. Three nights in, Durga's lesson is complete: she clears the road, she carries you across, and she comes again whenever she's remembered.

1112.title: Kushmanda's Smile, Lakshmi's Nights
1112.hook: night four: the list in the Devi Kavacha reaches Kushmanda, and in another way of keeping the festival, Durga's nights give way to Lakshmi's
1112.carry: one goddess: durga clears, then lakshmi fills
1112.howItsDone: Some Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga named in the Devi Kavacha on each night of Navaratri; others, especially in parts of South India, give three nights each to Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night three: the gods asked the goddess to come whenever they remember her, and Durga's nights closed. Tonight the lesson turns.
screen: `NIGHT THREE, DONE.` · `NIGHT FOUR.`

segments.voice: There's a short hymn called the Devi Kavacha, the goddess's armor, which some people recite before the Devi Mahatmya. Partway through, it counts the goddess out like stairs. First, Shailaputri. Second, Brahmacharini. Third, Chandraghanta. Fourth, Kushmanda. And on, name after name, until it says these are the nine Durgas. In some homes that list becomes the festival's calendar: one form for each night. But a second way of keeping Navaratri gives the first three nights to Durga, the middle three to Lakshmi, and the last three to Saraswati. By that count, night four is a hinge.
screen: `THE DEVI KAVACHA COUNTS HER OUT.` → `FOURTH: KUSHMANDA.` → `NIGHT FOUR IS A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Start with Kushmanda; you met her briefly on day ninety-four. The Kavacha only names her; it doesn't tell her story. But there's a story people tell. Before anything existed there was only darkness, and the goddess smiled, and the world came out of that smile. It's a bright picture for the fourth night: creation beginning as a face lighting up. Now the second way of counting. Durga's three nights cleared the road. Then, on night four, Lakshmi arrives: the goddess of good fortune, of plenty, of a household that has enough to share. Earlier this year, the Sri Sukta asked her to come and stay. Underneath both ways of counting is one Hindu teaching: the Devi is one, and she takes many forms. Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati aren't three rivals taking turns. Many devotees see them as faces of the one Shakti: power, plenty, and wisdom. Tradition even assigns the three parts of the Devi Mahatmya to Mahakali, Mahalakshmi and Mahasaraswati. So the order of the nights is the order of a life: clear what blocks the way, then let good things in, then learn. Some families have a homely version for tonight: before welcoming Lakshmi, they sweep the corners and light a lamp in a clean doorway, because Lakshmi, they say, comes to a home that's ready. And what she brings isn't more stuff. It's enough: health, a full table, friends at it, a little to give away. Kushmanda's smile sits over all of it: in this story the good world begins with delight.
screen: `FOURTH NIGHT: KUSHMANDA.` · `A WORLD FROM A SMILE.` · `ONE GODDESS, MANY FORMS.` · `DURGA CLEARS, LAKSHMI FILLS.` · then, large: `CLEAR, THEN FILL, THEN LEARN.`

segments.voice: Notice the room you're sitting in, the space around you and above you, the quiet between sounds, and let it feel roomy. Then let one good thing into that room, a person you're grateful for, a meal you're glad of, something already given, and let it sit there and be enough. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, quietly with the breath.

1113.title: Skandamata, Mother of Skanda
1113.hook: night five: dolls climb a set of steps in a living room, and the goddess of the night is a mother with her child on her lap
1113.carry: fierce and tender belong to one goddess
1113.howItsDone: In parts of South India, families set out a golu (kolu or bombe habba), a display of dolls on steps, for Navaratri and visit each other's homes in the evenings; where the nine forms are kept, the fifth night honors Skandamata.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night four: one goddess, Durga clearing and then Lakshmi filling. Tonight closes a week.
screen: `CLEARING FIRST, THEN FILLING.` · `NIGHT FIVE.`

segments.voice: In a living room in Chennai, someone has built a staircase out of planks and covered it with a cloth. On the steps stand dolls: gods near the top, saints and sages lower, then a wedding procession, a market, a cricket match, tiny clay animals. On the floor, a child has made a park out of sand, with a mirror for a pond. In parts of South India this is the golu, or kolu, set up for Navaratri. In the evenings neighbors come to see it, someone sings, and visitors leave with a small gift. And tonight, the fifth name in the Kavacha's list is a mother holding her child.
screen: `A STAIRCASE OF DOLLS.` → `NEIGHBORS COME TO SEE.` → `THE FIFTH NAME: A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Skandamata, the mother of Skanda. Skanda is the son of Shiva and Parvati, a young warrior god, known in the Tamil country as Murugan and elsewhere as Kartikeya, and his birth is a story of its own: the demon Taraka could be killed only by a son of Shiva, so the gods waited on that child, and he grew up to lead their army and win. In paintings of this night his mother sits with the boy on her lap. Notice what the name does. It doesn't call her by her own power. It calls her by the child she holds. And here's the teaching: in Hindu devotion the goddess who rides a lion into battle and the mother with a baby on her lap are not two goddesses. They're one. The fierce one is fierce for her children; the tender one is strong enough to have raised a god's general. The golu steps make a similar point with dolls. Gods at the top, then weddings, vegetable sellers, schoolchildren and cows: the whole ordinary world on the stairs, and neighbors come in to look. A festival about the goddess turns out to be full of visiting, feeding and children. A good end to a week that began with the goddess giving away her names, and ending them on mother. Halfway through the nine nights, the lesson so far: the power that clears the road is also the power that holds you.
screen: `SKANDAMATA, MOTHER OF SKANDA.` · `CALLED BY THE CHILD SHE HOLDS.` · `FIERCE AND TENDER, ONE GODDESS.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD ON THE STEPS.` · then, large: `THE POWER THAT HOLDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or someone who looks after you now, and stay with one moment of being cared for: a hand on your back, a plate put in front of you. Then, if it comes easily, let it turn around, and think of someone you hold, in whatever way you hold them. If you pray, you can offer both of them to the goddess, or to God, in your own words.
